lesson.subtitle: Lesson 7 -- From Founder to Seller
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Caio de Souza Amante | Lesson 7 -- From Founder to Seller
lesson.grammar_point: used to and would for past habits and states

listenings.text: The mistake is almost universal, and it comes from pride, which makes it very hard to argue with. You ask a founder to describe his company and he describes everything he still does. He is in every important client meeting. He reviews the pricing on every large proposal. He knows the name of every person in the building. He thinks he is describing commitment. What the buyer hears is that this company has exactly one point of failure, and it is sitting across the table. So I give my clients twenty minutes and two lists. The first list is what you did every single week five years ago. The second is what you do every week now. The gap between those two lists is the entire story, and it is the only part of the story a buyer is actually paying for. And I have never once had a founder who could not fill the first list. The problem is never that nothing changed. The problem is that nobody ever asked them to say it out loud, so they have no sentence ready on the day it matters.

I have bought eleven founder-led businesses and I ask the same question in every one of them. I ask the founder what he stopped doing. Then, and this is the part that matters, I ask four other people in the company the same question about him, separately, and I compare the answers. A founder who still does everything himself is a price problem, and I can solve a price problem. What actually worries me is the founder who tells me he handed something over, and then three of his own people tell me they still bring that decision back to him. That is not a price problem. That is a man who believes something about his own company that is not true, and I will find twenty more of those beliefs after I have paid for it. And here is the one that surprises people. When a founder tells me there is no single successor, that three people each hold a piece of it, I trust him more, not less. Inventing a name is easy. The invented name never survives the second meeting.

extra_audio.text: Let me answer that with what changed, not with a name. We bootstrapped the company, so for years I used to do all of it myself. I used to approve every hire, and the team leads have decided that since 2025. I did not use to delegate anything technical, and now I delegate all of it. So there is no single successor. Three people each own a piece of it. And the one thing I still do that I should not is read every proposal.
